title: No tracks
hook: a good traveler leaves no tracks, and the sage rejects no one (Tao Te Ching 27)

segments.voice: Yesterday, chapter twenty-six: heavy is the root, and your line was stillness masters. Were you the steady one in a room? Did the room follow? Day one thousand eighty-nine.

Early morning at a lakeside campsite. The tent is down and rolled. The fire ring is cold, the ashes scattered, the stones put back where they were found. Someone has walked the whole site once, head down, picking up a bottle cap and a twist tie that weren't even theirs. By the time the car pulls away, the clearing looks the way it did before they came, maybe a little better. The next family to arrive will never know anyone was there. Hikers have a phrase for this: leave no trace. Chapter twenty-seven of the Tao Te Ching says something like it, in its own way.
screen: `A CAMPSITE AT DAWN.` → `STONES PUT BACK.` → `LEAVE NO TRACE.`

segments.voice: First, no tracks, no tallies. In Legge's translation, the chapter opens: "The skilful traveller leaves no traces of his wheels or footsteps." Then a list in the same key. A good speaker says nothing anyone can find fault with. A good counter needs no tally sticks. The skill is so complete you can't see the machinery. Second, locks without bolts. The list goes on. A good closer shuts a door with no bolt, and still it can't be opened. A good binder ties with no rope, and still it can't be undone. What holds things together here isn't hardware. It's something quieter, like trust, or care so thorough it doesn't need a padlock. Third, no one thrown away. Then the chapter turns to people. The sage, it says, is good at saving people, and so no one is cast away. Good at saving things, and so nothing is thrown out. No one is written off as a lost cause. The chapter gives this a name, which translators render in different ways; some hear in it a hidden light. Fourth, teacher and material. The chapter ends with a pairing that can surprise. The good person is the teacher of the one who isn't good. And the one who isn't good is the good person's material, what they have to work with. If you don't honor your teacher, and don't care for your material, the chapter says, then however clever you are, you are badly lost. Leaving no tracks, it turns out, isn't only about tidiness. It's about doing good so quietly that nobody is rejected, and nobody is left owing.
screen: `NO TRACKS, NO TALLIES.` · `LOCKS WITHOUT BOLTS.` · `NO ONE THROWN AWAY.` · `TEACHER AND MATERIAL.` · then, large: `NO TRACKS, AND NO ONE CAST AWAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: choose a place to leave better, without being seen. Settle, and breathe. Think through the places you'll pass through today: a shared kitchen, a bathroom at work, a bus seat, a sidewalk, a friend's couch. Pick one. Now decide on one small thing you'll do there: wipe the counter, straighten the chairs, pick up what someone dropped. Picture yourself doing it and walking away, with nobody thanking you, and nothing to show. The bell holds the time.
No tracks. Chapter twenty-seven's skilled traveler, who leaves no trace, and its sage, who throws no one away. Today's word.
Your line: no tracks. Do the thing you chose, leave the place better, and don't mention it to anyone. Day one thousand eighty-nine.

howItsDone: Some readers of the Tao Te Ching put chapter twenty-seven into practice through small unseen acts of care, tidying, repairing, helping, done without leaving any mark of who did them.

myth: chapter twenty-seven says the sage gives up on people who can't be helped
the sage is good at saving people, so no one is cast away.
the chapter calls the one who isn't good the good person's material
the good person is the teacher; the one who isn't good is what the good person has to work with.
in this chapter, a good closer needs a strong lock
a good closer shuts a door with no bolt, and still it can't be opened.

fork.setup: you're the sage of chapter twenty-seven, and someone in your town is known as a lost cause. what do you do?
options: keep them out, for everyone's sake.
save them, because the sage casts no one away.
wait for them to fix themselves.
fork.reveal: the sage is good at saving people, and so no one is cast away. even the one who isn't good is called the good person's material.

original.note: Chinese, shàn xíng wú zhé jì: good travel leaves no wheel tracks. The opening of Tao Te Ching 27.

trapdoor: what you thought: no tracks means be sneaky.
what it means: skill so complete it leaves no trace, and a sage who throws no one away.
what a scholar hears: shan xing wu zhe ji, no wheel ruts, then the pairing of the good as teacher and the not-good as material.

sources.quoted: The skilful traveller leaves no traces of his wheels or footsteps

sources.ref: Tao Te Ching, chapter 27 (speaker, counter, closer, binder; saving people and things; teacher and material)

notes: Verify the Legge 1891 wording: 'The skilful traveller leaves no traces of his wheels or footsteps'.
The rest of chapter 27 is paraphrased. 襲明 is rendered as 'following the light, a kind of hidden brightness' (Legge: 'hiding the light of his procedure'); confirm.
'Leave no trace' is cited as a hikers' phrase, not as a source. The hook links the modern phrase to the chapter without any claim about history or influence.
The campsite scene is an illustration, not a source.
Pronunciation guide for 善行無轍迹 is approximate.

Editor: brought the speaker line closer to the text (Legge: nothing that can be found fault with); replaced 'following the light, a kind of hidden brightness' with a hedged 'some hear in it a hidden light' (襲明, Legge: 'hiding the light of his procedure'); smoothed the closing 'nobody gets a bill'.
